children.text: This is Latino USA, the radio journal of news and culture.

I'm Maria Hinojosa. This time on Latino USA, the people on the Puerto Rican island of Vieques vote to evict the U.S. Navy. So, what now happens is the people of Puerto Rico has expressed their will. The Navy now is withdrawing from its commitment to hold a referendum, and everything is now up in the air again. Also, Peru's new president carries the hopes of its nation's poor. I think a lot of people out there believe in him and really hope that as someone who came up from a really poor background, that he will do something for them. I think there's a lot of expectation now. We have five years to see what happens. This and more coming up on this edition of Latino USA.

For this week, this is news from Latino USA. I'm Maria Martin. Some House Democrats have outlined a comprehensive immigration plan, which includes unionizing guest workers and increasing the number of visas available for Mexican and Canadian immigrants. Patricia Guadalupe has more from Washington. The plan recommends granting legal permanent residency to undocumented immigrants who have been in the United States since before January of this year. It also includes setting up a temporary guest worker program and recommends lifting immigrant visa requirements for Mexicans as a way to reunite more families. The proposals are not part of any legislative package yet, but sponsors hope to include them in a Bush administration plan that the White House wants to have in place when Mexican President Vicente Fox visits Washington on September 5th. For Latino USA, this is Patricia Guadalupe in Washington.

As the debate continues in Washington over whether Mexican trucks can come into this country, President Vicente Fox of Mexico said he would close his country's borders to American trucks if the U.S. fails to comply with the terms of the North American Free Trade Agreement. More from Latino USA's Franc Contreras in Mexico. President Fox's remarks follow demands by the Mexican Congress, which opposes any restrictions preventing Mexican trucks from entering the U.S. Fox first hinted that Mexico might use the NAFTA treaty and impose billions of dollars in sanctions against the United States. Observers thought Fox would not risk upsetting the U.S. and lose a possible immigration accord, but his recent comments suggest otherwise.

Meanwhile, Mexico's largest trucking association says its long-haul trucks are safe enough to travel inside the U.S. Trucking firms here know that the Teamsters Union is lobbying to block Mexican trucks because the Teamsters fear losing jobs to lower-paid foreign drivers. Mexican truckers, though, are taking advantage of the delay. They're learning U.S. road regulations and preparing to compete in the U.S. transportation market. For Latino USA, this is Franc Contreras in Oaxaca City, Mexico. Texas State officials will begin a criminal investigation into whether Houston hospitals are breaking the law by providing non-emergency health care to undocumented immigrants. Latino USA's Deepa Dande has more.

This investigation follows a legal opinion by state Attorney General John Cornyn, who recently stated that the Personal Responsibility and Reconciliation Act of 1996 bars the district from providing preventative care to the state's undocumented population. Frumencio Reyes, Chair of Houston Mayor's Hispanic Advisory Committee, says many Latino civil rights groups and immigrant advocates were surprised by what they call a sudden decision. It certainly has a very chilling effect. Not only the immigrant community, but the community as a whole is going to be impacted. LULAC, the League of United Latin American Citizens, is working with lawmakers, immigrant advocates, and civil rights organizations to come up with a reasonable alternative. For Latino USA, I'm Deepa Dande. This is news from Latino USA.

Cancer is forcing Bolivia's President General Hugo Banzer to resign from office. The former dictator and now elected president, Banzer is voluntarily handing over the reins of power to Vice President Jorge Quiroga on August 6th, Bolivia's Independence Day. Vanessa Arrington reports from La Paz. A graduate of Texas A&M and former IBM executive, Jorge Quiroga is no stranger to the United States. Only a few Bolivian presidents have received American college degrees. Quiroga's wife, Virginia, a Texan, will be the country's first-ever American first lady. The 41-year-old Quiroga has been described by his supporters as intelligent and one of Bolivia's few honest politicians.

Quiroga will continue Banzer's controversial initiative to eradicate coca, the plant that is used to make cocaine. He also will work to secure plans for exporting Bolivia's natural gas. Quiroga will be in power until the next presidential election, which is scheduled to take place in June of 2002. For Latino USA, I'm Vanessa Arrington in La Paz, Bolivia. A mass campaign to register Hispanic voters in Georgia has announced it has run out of money and will have to close up shop. From Atlanta, Georgia Public Radio's Maura Farrelly reports. Georgia's Hispanic voter registration campaign was founded in 1999 with a $100,000 grant from the private foundation led by Jane Fonda.

Since that time, the campaign's Executive Director, Sora Chavez McFarlane, has registered nearly 14,000 Georgians to vote. McFarlane says the most disturbing thing about the current situation is that business leaders in the Hispanic community were unwilling to help her when she asked for donations. Sounds like in our community, when you get a little job and you dress a little well, then you don't want to see the rest, the Latinos. And that's a big mistake. McFarlane says that of the nearly 700 members of the Georgia Hispanic Chamber of Commerce, just three contributed financially to the campaign. For Latino USA, I'm Maura Farrelly. In Austin, Texas, I'm Maria Martin. You're listening to Latino USA.

I'm Maria Hinojosa. As this program goes to air, the U.S. Armed Services Committee was holding hearings on the issue of the Naval base on the Puerto Rican island of Vieques. This following a referendum in which 68% of the residents of Vieques voted to end all Naval exercises immediately. The Bush administration has not changed its position of halting Naval exercises, but only two years from now. Joining us from San Juan, Puerto Rico, to figure out what's next in the ongoing drama of Vieques is Political Analyst Juan Manuel Garcia Passalacqua. Juanma, bienvenido de nuevo a Latino USA. Let's talk about this most recent referendum.

68% of the Viequenses voted to end the Navy's presence on the island immediately, but this was a non-binding referendum. So what purpose, if any, did this vote serve, and what was the reaction of the Bush administration? Well, Maria, it's a pleasure to be with you, as always. And let me tell you, this is the biggest confrontation between the United States and Puerto Rico in 102 years. The Armed Services Committee has recommended to the whole Congress that the referendum the Navy wanted, the referendum that was going to be binding in November, be abolished, because now they know they're going to lose it seven to three.

So, what now happens is the people of Puerto Rico has expressed their will. The Navy now is withdrawing from its commitment to hold a referendum, and everything is now up in the air again. Well, so what purpose did the vote serve? Who called this vote, and does this, again, point to this very particular relationship the United States and Puerto Rico have? That Puerto Rico is a somewhat independent Republic, but is really subjugated to the United States on all counts. Well, you're familiar with that story for years, Maria, and that's exactly the point. The White House said this week that if Puerto Rico were a nation, the people of that nation would have something to say regarding foreign bases on its soil.

And that if Puerto Rico was a U.S. community, the U.S. community would have something to say, but since Puerto Rico is neither, no one is going to pay attention to the referendum held here at the initiative of the governor to strengthen the hand of the Puerto Rican people vis-à-vis the White House and the Congress. Now, there are reports that pro-Navy supporters in Puerto Rico are trying to paint those opposed to the military presence in Vieques as communists, as un-American Puerto Rican separatists. Is there such a smear campaign going on now? Are you seeing a heightened presence on the part of these pro-Navy supporters?

That was the campaign. For the whole month of campaigning, there were all sorts of signs in Vieques saying, if the Navy loses, Fidel Castro will come to Vieques on Monday, but that didn't work. The Navy got only 30%. It was a disaster for them, so it's over. I mean, the people of Vieques have spoken, and now the Congress is saying, we're scrapping referendums here. We're just waiting for the Navy to tell us what to do. Now, what happens next, Juan Manuel? Will there, in fact, be any referendum on the island of Vieques about Vieques that will be supported by the Navy? Will there be an increased presence of demonstrations? I mean, you've been watching this for the past several years.

Will there be a shift here? Where are we moving towards? I have no doubt whatsoever that the electoral victory has galvanized the opposition to the Navy, and you're going to get, at least, 300 to 500 more protesters inside the camp next week when the Navy begins to bomb again. There have already been 1,300 arrests, and there have been about 400 trials already, so now you're going to get that multiplied.

And that's why the Armed Services Committee said, forget the referendum, forget everything. Let the Navy say what they want to do now. The Navy will have to make a determination. If they don't leave now and fulfill the will of the people, they will be facing one of the most dangerous situations in Amritsar in India, or Sétif in Algeria, or Belfast in Northern Ireland. Well, thanks very much for speaking with us. Juan Manuel Garcia Passalacqua is a senior political analyst based in San Juan, Puerto Rico.

In just one year, Peru's political landscape has completely been transformed. Not only has disgraced ex-president Alberto Fujimori fled to Japan, but he's been replaced by the man who led last year's street protests against him, Alejandro Toledo. Born into poverty, Toledo is Peru's first president to identify himself with his own Indigenous roots. At his recent inauguration ceremonies, Toledo announced a pact with other Andean nations to respect the rights, cultures, and traditions of Indigenous peoples. Correspondent Tatiana Harrison reports on the events that kicked off what Peruvians hope will be a new political era in their country.

The swearing-in of Alejandro Toledo may not have had the angry street protests of last year during ex-president Alberto Fujimori's controversial inauguration, but it was not without its contentious moments. “Witches get rid of those witches,” shout Toledo supporters from the balconies of Congress during his inauguration speech. The witches were the three remaining congresswomen of Fujimori's once-powerful party. They were holding up signs saying, “Fujimori pacified the nation” or “DNA,” referring to campaign-season reports that Toledo had fathered an illegitimate child he refuses to recognize. This year, Fujimori supporters were the heckling minority.

But not long ago, Fujimori and his spy chief, Vladimiro Montesinos, were the supreme authority, with video footage showing they had bought out media, business, and political figures. But less than a year later, Fujimori would be exiled in Japan, Montesinos in jail, and Peruvians were tuning in to watch a peaceful transfer of power. Just hours before handing over the presidential sash to Alejandro Toledo, Interim President Valentín Paniagua arrived at the Cathedral of Lima for an early mass. Paniagua had presided over a transitional government that held elections widely considered free of corruption. Toledo, a former World Bank economist, won by a thin margin.

The Paniagua-led government also launched hundreds of investigations into corrupt officials, and many are already behind bars, including Blanca Nélida Colán, the former attorney general under Fujimori. Toledo, the first Peruvian president with humble roots and Indigenous blood, has represented his government as market economics with a human face. Although his cabinet is headed up by big-business-friendly ministers, in his inauguration speech, he often referred to himself as the president of the poor. “We will reduce poverty. That is the central task of my government.” The day after this speech, Toledo flew to the ancient Incan capital of Cusco.

Toledo flew to the ancient Incan capital of Cusco to fulfill a campaign promise to hold a second symbolic inauguration at the ruins of the mountain citadel of Machu Picchu. Standing among the lush peaks surrounding Machu Picchu, journalist Lucien Chauvin, who's been covering Peru for 12 years, says many grassroots leaders are relying on Toledo's success to ascend in the political power structure. A lot of people out there believe in him and really hope that as someone who came up from a really poor background, that he will do something for them. There's a lot of expectation now, although we have five years to see what happens.

If he fails, people are going to say, see, someone of Indigenous heritage is incapable of running a country. One person who thinks Toledo's gotten off on a good foot is Nobel Laureate Shimon Peres, who was a special guest at the invitation-only event at Machu Picchu. “And I wish you all the best. It's a new chapter in the history of Peru, to become democratic, to become modern, to combine an old culture with a new economy.” Toledo faces some high hurdles in making this combination work.

While dealing with the pressures to service its $27 billion external debt, the government must respond to Peru's poor, which comprise 54% of the population, most of them of Indigenous descent, who are crying out for relief and jobs. Toledo plans to tackle this by introducing many immediate measures to reactivate the economy, such as increasing corporate taxes, lowering sales taxes, and creating government programs to help people buy homes, spurring the construction sector. Despite the huge economic obstacles, Toledo clearly carries the hope of the masses. Alzida Alza Alcatriz was among those who helped Toledo celebrate his first day in office at an outdoor rally just after the Machu Picchu ceremony.

Sitting among her potatoes at Cusco's Central Market, she was filled with joy that Toledo traveled to be with the Cusconians. “I'm encouraged because he has suffered as a kid, and he's authentic Andean like us. He hasn't lost his customs, and he's proud of the life he's had. He has Andean blood like us.” Several rows down, sitting a stone's throw from the pig snouts and cow tails of the market, Julia says she was impressed by his promises to be president of the poor, as the poor have always been forgotten in Peru, but she worries that people will just expect handouts from the new president.

“If we want him to be a good president, we have to work. That's the only way we can get out of this poverty.” Julia and millions of other Peruvians, sick of lies and false promises, will be vigilant in holding Toledo to his victory-speech pledge on election night, when he announced that he would never let them down. For Latino USA, this is Tatiana Harrison in Lima, Peru. Are you sitting comfortably? Then I'll begin. Alejandro Amenábar is a film director, screenwriter, and music composer.

Born in Chile and raised in Spain, Amenábar has written, directed, and scored two critically acclaimed films from Spain. His first, Tésis, won seven Spanish Academy Awards in 1995, and his second, Abre Los Ojos, is one of Spain's highest-grossing movies of all time. His first English-language feature film, entitled The Others, opens August 10th, and we're pleased to welcome Alejandro Amenábar to our studio. Alejandro, bienvenido a Latino USA.

Now, The Others, which, of course, it worked out so well because just before I came to this interview last night, I saw a trailer for your film, which sent me shivering and thanking that my kids did not see it. It's a frightening trailer. The film stars Nicole Kidman. Tom Cruise is one of the producers. So, tell us the story of how a relatively unknown Spanish-language director like yourself manages to get the attention of some of these big-time Hollywood heavyweights. Well, I guess it's about just delivering them my work. My second film was presented at Sundance a few years ago, and Tom Cruise and Paula Wagner watched the film, and they really loved it, so they got the rights.

In the meantime, I wrote this story for The Others. We translated it into English. We sent it here to a few companies, including, of course, Cruise/Wagner, and they and Miramax were really interested in the project. Well, what do you think it was? There are a lot of scary movies out there. What is it about this particular film that you think stands out? It plays in a different way compared to many horror films nowadays, which is playing with special effects and sound effects. So, this film plays with very primary and basic fears in an internal way, and with the psychology of the audience. That's the way it works at a much quieter level, playing with silence, with not the kind of things you would expect in a horror film nowadays.

So, how did you capture that, and also, what was the inspiration? I'll tell you one of the last scary films that I saw that I loved because of the fact that it had so few special effects, was The Shining, and it had that element of silence, that element of the long hallways. Tell us a little bit about this one. Yeah, exactly. It's in my case, when I was writing, I was just trying to put myself as a child, trying to remember the shivers that I used to have when I was a child.

And basically, it had to do mostly with darkness and with ghosts, but basically, with unseen things, with everything that is hidden, that is behind doors, that is in almost darkness. Tell us what it was like working with Nicole Kidman and Tom Cruise. Well, it has been an incredible experience for me. Nicole is an excellent actress, and we had a very creative relationship. She always understood the film that I wanted to make, and I always understood that she needed freedom and space to create her character.

And Tom, he's an executive producer of the film, and he has been very supportive and making sure that I wouldn't miss anything during the whole process. And I was very open to any of his suggestions. Now, there have been a number of great filmmakers who direct, but really very few who actually compose their own musical score. And how did you get this multifaceted background in not only literature and graphic arts, but also music? When I was a child, I started to write, to do drawings, and to compose music for my drawings. I never studied music, but I used to play the guitar and the keyboards.

And now I help myself nowadays with a computer, a multi-track system, and I do all my work in my office. And then the music has to be performed by an orchestra. All that is transferred, but it's a process that has been really interesting for me. It helps me to set the whole tone and the mood of the film. So, we've seen some recent crossovers from Spain here. Antonio Banderas, Penélope Cruz, are you thinking that you, Alejandro Amenábar, are going to be the next Almodóvar?

Or is this a one-shot deal? Let me do this, but then you really want to maintain yourself focused in Spain and the work that you're doing? Well, actually, I think that Almodóvar has been able to maintain the nature of his films, and he actually hasn't shot yet in English. And it's very right. You have to be very careful. Hollywood can be really a field of dreams, or can be a nightmare for many directors. So I've seen many frustrated directors, foreign directors, who come to Hollywood expecting to really do at last the film they wanted to, and they end up doing something that they are not proud of at all, so you have to be very careful with that.

Last thing. Just the last line. “Can't you hear it?” “Scare me for one minute.” “Is someone there?” It's very difficult for me to scare you. So, tell me one line that's going to scare me if I— Well, there's one line that many people love in the film. It says, “Sometimes I bleed.” And actually, Nicole usually says, “I bled for this character.” “Where is my daughter?” “Are you mad? I am your daughter.” Oh, okay. Well, thanks very much for joining us. We've been speaking with Alejandro Amenábar, screenwriter, film director, and musical composer. His new film, The Others, stars Nicole Kidman and begins a national release in August.

Most Americans view the current Bush administration immigration reform proposal through the rather limited lens of domestic policy. Latinos, on the other hand, will evaluate the regularization, or amnesty proposal, with an eye to how it impacts us and how it affects our families and friends in América Latina. The Bush administration is currently considering a proposal to grant legal status to a number of undocumented immigrants already living and working in the United States. Commentator Roberto Lovato has some thoughts on the latest immigration proposals being considered by the White House and their connection to U.S. foreign policy.

In the new globalized world, most Latinos view those border crossers some condemn as criminals with compassion and memory. We are keenly, often painfully aware of the relationship between foreign policy and domestic immigration law, and we can also provide insight as to who is the real criminal and who really deserves amnesty. We remember the past. The civil wars in Central America that led millions to vote with their feet and flee oppressive systems and violence. Viewed from this perspective, many Americans, including myself, are asking this question: don't the administration's immigration proposals strike a disturbing note when set against recent appointments and nominations to key posts affecting Latin America policy?

With the nomination of some former Reagan administration officials, Cold War rhetoric and tensions have resurfaced. Many believe that John Negroponte, Otto Reich, and Elliott Abrams were an important part of a U.S. Central America policy that resulted in the subversion of U.S. laws and in the torture, disappearance, and death of hundreds of thousands in Guatemala, El Salvador, Nicaragua, and Honduras. Of the three, only Abrams is a convicted criminal. He confessed to two lesser counts of deceiving Congress in sworn testimony during the Iran-Contra scandal, and was later given amnesty by the former President Bush.

These appointments raise more questions. Do they reveal a more sinister, cynical side of compassionate conservatism? The whole of Latin America awaits an answer, as does our conscience as a country and our desire to see a day when no more millions flee their homelands only to be labeled criminals because we ourselves were born of constant global shifts dating back centuries. Latinos in the United States are uniquely positioned to understand the relationship between domestic immigration policy and foreign policy. It behooves us to learn about and weigh in on these critical appointments and nominations. At a time when everybody seems to want our vote, just what is the message the administration is sending with these appointments? Commentator Roberto Lovato heads the recently created Central American Studies Program at California State University at Northridge.

And for this week, this has been Latino USA, the radio journal of news and culture. Thanks for listening. Gracias por escucharnos.
